newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Slovak stock market overshadowed by new law.
newsitem.headline: Slovak stock market overshadowed by new law.

text.p: A new securities law has dealt a severe blow to Slovakia's capital markets and, coupled with recent central bank monetary measures, could leave them struggling to recover, analysts said on Tuesday.
The law allows majority shareholders to arbitrarily suspend stock market trading in their shares.
"If nothing changes for the better, our capital market will need at least half a year to recover from this blow," said Vladimir Kuklis, an analyst at CSOB bank.

Parliamentary approval in October of the securities law and new central bank capital adequacy rules excluding foreign exchange held locally then added to the market's woes, as did signs of a slowing economy, the analysts said.
Slovak shares had already started to fall at the end of August after the privatisation of blue chip oil and gas storage company Nafta which was sold below its market value.

"The privatisation of Nafta deeply shook foreign investors," said Martin Barto of ING Barings. "The slow-down in the GDP growth and the precarious trade balance would in themselves be enough to pull the market down."
"But add to that the non-standard amendment to the securities law which spread so much uncertainty, and I see a really gloomy future for the market at least in the short-term," he continued.
CSOB's Kuklis said current credit interest rates of around 15 percent were also a major obstacle to significant new investment in the cash-starved market.
And the prospect of a further rate rise due to central bank measures aimed at curbing loan expansion -- due to take effect from 1997 -- has made the outlook even more pessimistic.
"It is hard to predict when rates may ease, but I am afraid that the entire package bodes drastically ill for further development of the whole economy," Kuklis said.

Legislative barriers have also held up some investors, analysts said, since Slovak law requires shares to be held for at least a year before they are recognised as a portfolio investment and so can qualify for value-added-tax relief.
